open_points.subject: scratch file-size limit outcome
open_points.text: “the runner ignores the signal the host sends for a write past it, so the write fails with an error the code can see” and “a limit hit (memory, process count, scratch, `output_bytes`) — `resource_exhausted`”
open_points.question: When code attempts to grow a scratch file past `sandbox_scratch_bytes_max` but catches the resulting write error and returns conforming outputs, how does the runner detect the limit hit, and is the execution `resource_exhausted` or `succeeded`?
options: Every attempted over-limit write is reported out of band and forces `resource_exhausted` even if caught
Only an uncaught write failure affects the outcome, normally as `crashed`; caught failures may still succeed
A caught write failure still forces `resource_exhausted` by some other specified observation
open_points.default_guess: Report the attempted breach out of band and return `resource_exhausted`, preserving the stated outcome precedence.

open_points.subject: meaning of a scratch limit hit
open_points.text: “the directory as a whole has no separate bound in this release” and “a limit hit (memory, process count, scratch, `output_bytes`) — `resource_exhausted`”
open_points.question: With no total directory bound, does “scratch” in the outcome rule mean only an `RLIMIT_FSIZE` breach, or also host filesystem failures such as exhausted space, quota, or inodes; and how are caught versus uncaught such failures classified?
options: Only `RLIMIT_FSIZE` is the scratch limit; host-capacity errors follow ordinary caught/uncaught code behavior
Any inability to write in the scratch is `resource_exhausted`
Configured file-size breaches are `resource_exhausted`, while host-capacity failures are `crashed` even if code catches them
open_points.default_guess: Treat only an observed `RLIMIT_FSIZE` breach as the scratch limit; ordinary filesystem-capacity errors remain visible to code and become `crashed` only if uncaught.
